name: A-Hmao, Eastern

PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 339 pp. (open PDF, cs.cmu.edu/~dmortens; eScholarship qt0sp1b9w8). The A-Hmao data and the stress remark are credited to Wang Fushi & Wang Deguang 1996, Guizhou Weining Miaoyu dai qianjia chengfen de shuangyinjie mingci de xingtai bianhua, Minzu Yuwen 1996(1): 34-36 (not reachable).
catalog_locator: p. 197 (printed; p. 213), Chapter 5, sec. 5.1.2.3, paragraph between examples (143) and (144); supporting: sec. 2.4 pp. 38-39, examples (39a-b); sec. 6.3.1 pp. 284-286
catalog_quote: Both of them enforce a difference in only one vowel of the conjunct. In both cases, this is the tonic vowel. For A-Hmao, this is the vowel in the root, which is always the last vowel in a noun. All of the nouns that participate in this construct are reportedly iambs, with an unstressed prefix as the first syllable. In English, each conjunct is typically a trochee, or—if the conjunct is monosyllabic—a single, stressed syllable.
sweep_summary: Diandongbei-Large Flowery Miao is not in the catalog and this search of works with stress in the title produced exactly one title hit, Vogel (2023) 'Is There Foot Structure in Isolating Languages?', which Glottolog itself flags as a computerized language assignment from the word 'isolating'. Its abstract (OpenAlex, saved) says the two languages examined are Mandarin Chinese and Vietnamese; it is paywalled (DOI 10.1515/9783110730081-005; Unpaywall closed, no open copy found via OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, archive.org or Google Books). Relevance to this language: none; no first-hand stress statement for larg1235 was read.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In prefixed disyllabic nouns (the only common polysyllabic native word type besides compounds) the nominal prefix is unstressed and the root syllable, always the final syllable of the noun, carries the stress (iambic prefix+root). The language is otherwise tonal (six tones with breathy-voice register per Gerner 2019 p. 66); no source opened states anything about stress in monosyllables, compounds, or at phrase level.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the remark is hedged ('reportedly') and covers only the prefix+root nouns that undergo echo reduplication. Ratliff 2010 (Hmong-Mien Language History, PL 613, p. 199, held by the project under hmon1333) makes the same claim at family level: Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes 'are unstressed, and in some languages they may harmonize with the nouns to which they are attached (Chen 1993)', with Shimen (A-Hmao) prefixed forms a1-və1 'stone', a1-mpy6 'nose' cited on p. 201.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: prefix+root nouns (e.g. a55-ma53 'eye', ki-tu 'horn' in Mortensen's examples pp. 285-286). Not a first-hand description: Mortensen analyses published data (Wang & Wang 1986, 1996; Johnson 1999) and marks the stress claim 'reportedly'. Tonal language; the statement concerns the prosodic weakness of the prefix syllable, not a general word-stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The Mortensen 2006 material is Eastern A-Hmao (Shimenkan township, Weining county, Guizhou; the Pollard-script standard point) and Western A-Hmao (Johnson 1999), both within larg1235 [hmd]; Gerner 2019 and Gerner & Bisang describe Weining Ahmao, same languoid. No separate glottocode for these dialects.
